catalog_quote: Une syllabe finale est toujours accentuée devant pause (externe ou interne) : elle est prononcée avec plus de force et surtout, elle est toujours vocalisée, qu'elle se termine par une syllabe ouverte : (C)CV, ou fermée : (C)CVC. C'est ainsi que nous analysons les syllabes finales (C)CVC comme des réalisations pausales accentuées de (C)CC avec épenthèse. La position de l'accent d'intensité est fixe et systématique devant pause; il n'est donc pas distinctif. (p. 445) ... Devant pause, un accent d'intensité se porte automatiquement sur la syllabe finale, ouverte ou fermée, ce qui entraîne la règle d'épenthèse pausale ... Toute syllabe devant pause (interne ou externe) est accentuée (p. 456) ... Dans les schèmes tonals de base, il faut observer qu'il n'y a qu'un seul ton haut dans chaque structure. Comme nous le verrons par la suite, le ton haut entraînant systématiquement une tension vocal…
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Mofu-Gudur is not in the catalog. The single stress-title item, Glottolog ref 156268 'Hollingsworth 1990, A study of tone, stress and intonation in Mofu-Gudur', was located in the SIL Language & Culture Archives (entry 47707): it is a 9-page SIL Cameroon draft typescript dated November 1980 (Glottolog's 1990 is a mis-date), with an open PDF (scanned, no text layer). sil.org is an automated-access block-could not be reached by automated download, so the record page and PDF were downloaded from the Internet Archive (snapshots 2024-08-17/18), scanned with tesseract at 300 dpi one page at a time, and key quotes checked against the page images; everything is and logged in there. The paper says Mofu-Gudur is a two-tone (H/L) language 'which also exhibits stress', but the stress it describes is utterance-level 'center of information stress' (extra-high pitch on a speaker-chosen word, predicted in narrative by a ranking vocatives > ideophones > location NP > verb > time words > pause particle > nouns) plus sentence-final intonation; at word level it only notes that drift can be overridden by stress and that rules could not yet be formulated. It states no fixed word-stress position, so it is classed prosody-but-not-word-stress and bears no-catalog-record. The best first-hand word-level statement read in this search of works with stress in the title remains Barreteau 1988 Livre 1 pp. 445-446/456 (already held by the project from our earlier reading): an automatic, fixed, non-distinctive intensity accent on the final syllable before pause. nothing remains to acquire for this language.

Dans un lexème verbal, l'accent peut être absent ; il peut précéder la première consonne, se situer sur la voyelle interne ou être placé après la dernière consonne du thème verbal. (p. 366)
new_statements.translation: A final syllable is always accented before a pause (external or internal): it is pronounced with more force and, above all, it is always vocalised, whether it ends in an open syllable (C)CV or a closed one (C)CVC. [...] The position of the intensity accent is fixed and systematic before pause; it is therefore not distinctive. (p. 445) — Before pause, an intensity accent falls automatically on the final syllable, open or closed, which triggers the pausal epenthesis rule (p. 456) — [...] there is reason to speak here of accent or tonal accent rather than of tone. In a verbal lexeme the accent may be absent; it may precede the first consonant, sit on the internal vowel, or be placed after the last consonant of the verb stem. (p. 366)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mofu-Gudur is a two-tone language (H vs B, H marked). Barreteau distinguishes two things: (1) a lexical 'accent tonal' = the single H that a basic non-derived word may carry (none, initial, internal or final: schemes BBB / HBB, BHB, BBH), which is lexically distributed, i.e. tone; (2) a non-distinctive 'accent d'intensité' (stress) that falls automatically on the final syllable of any phonological word before a pause, external or internal (e.g. between reduplicated parts), forcing vocalisation of that syllable. So word-level stress, where it exists, is fixed final and predictable (pausal/phrase-final), not contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. In complex (prefixed/reduplicated) words each pre-pausal syllable (before internal virtual pause or semi-pause) is accented, giving several accented syllables; in rapid speech the semi-pause and its accent disappear (pp. 447-448).
new_statements.exceptions: Intensity accent is tied to pause: a final syllable not before pause (in context) is not accented and may stay non-vocalised (C)CC. H-tone 'accent tonal' is absent in all-low words; verbs are cited with prefix me- and suffix -ey, and derived words can carry several H tones.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'mot phonologique' (simple = non-derived base; complex = derived by prefixation/reduplication) in pausal position: the accent is a phrase-final/pausal phenomenon, and Barreteau explicitly says it is not distinctive. The lexical prominence is tonal; Barreteau's 'accent tonal' is his reinterpretation of the single H in basic tone schemes, not a stress observation. Dialect described: Mofu-Gudur of Mokong (Mofou-Nord/Mokong and Mofou-Sud cantons, Mayo-Tsanaga).
new_statements.identity_note: Barreteau describes Mofu-Gudur proper (mofu-sud, ALCAM 178, ISO mif = glottocode mofu1248) as spoken at Mokong (Mofou-Nord/Mokong and Mofou-Sud cantons, Mayo-Tsanaga, Far North Cameroon), explicitly distinguished from the northern 'Mofu' of Méri (North Mofu, nort3046). The 1978 chapter title 'mofu-gadar' in Glottolog is a typo for mofu-gudur (the IRD copy reads MOFU-GUDUR).

new_statements.reading: Mofu-Gudur is a two-tone language; besides tone it has a fixed, non-distinctive intensity accent on the final syllable of the phonological word when that word stands before a pause (i.e. phrase/utterance-final position; the verbal complex thus stresses its last suffix, p. 451). Word-final, automatic, non-contrastive. Hollingsworth 1980 (the works with stress in the title, now downloaded) adds a separate utterance-level focal 'center of information stress' realized as extra-high pitch, assignable to almost any word and governed in discourse by a grammatical-category ranking; it states no fixed word-level position. Barreteau 1988 remains the first-hand statement of word-level accent placement.

new_statements.quote: Mofu-Gudur, a Chadic family language spoken in northern Cameroun, is a tonal language which also exhibits stress. [p. 1] — The super high is attributed to stress given by a speaker. [...] While in Mofu a speaker may assign stress to most any word in the utterance (or not assign stress to any word), the general pattern for assigning stress in a narrative discourse can be predicted on the basis of a hierarchy or ranking of grammatical categories. [p. 5] — Mofu-Gudur, while a tonal language, also has stress which influences the tone on the word, phrase, and sentence levels. On an utterance in a discourse stress is frequently predictable on the basis of grammatical criteria. [p. 9]

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with, and already summarized in, the existing statements: it adds an utterance-level focal prominence (super-high pitch, grammatical-category ranking) on top of tone, but states no fixed word-level stress position, so it neither confirms nor contradicts Barreteau 1988's automatic, non-distinctive intensity accent on the final syllable before pause (Livre 1 pp. 445-446, 456).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two-tone language (H, L; about a dozen noun minimal pairs). The 'stress' Hollingsworth describes is not a fixed word-level position: it is one focal 'center of information stress' per utterance, realized as a super-high pitch (a H raised above other Hs, or a L turned H), assignable by the speaker to almost any word or to none; in narrative discourse its placement follows a ranking of grammatical categories (1 vocatives, 2 ideophones, 3 location NP, 4 verb, 5 time words/adverbs, 6 the pause particle, 7 nouns; pp. 7-8). At word level he only notes (p. 2) that stress can override up/downdrift and that a low-tone schwa in a 3-syllable LLL word can take a stress that makes it seem high; 'not enough data has been observed as yet to formulate rules'. Sentence intonation (p. 8): a rise 2-3 syllables from the end over a H, last syllable lowest and usually falling. No statement of where word stress falls.
new_statements.exceptions: Isolated elicited sentences can violate the ranking since stress can be voluntarily shifted; ideophone kew 'hitting sound' shifts its stress and tone to the next syllable to the right (p. 7); verb low-tone schwa may optionally be high in the Mokong dialect and is always high in the Gudal dialect (p. 3).
new_statements.identity_note: Hollingsworth 1980 mentions two Mofu-Gudur dialects, Mokong and Gudal, only for a verb-tone detail (p. 3); otherwise it treats the language as a whole. Wolff 1987 concerns Lamang, Podoko, Musgu, Masa, Zime, Lame, Kera, Kwang, Tobanga, Ngizim, Bade, Bole and Kanakuru, not Mofu-Gudur.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction. Wolff 1987 is not about Mofu-Gudur at all (13 other Chadic languages), so it neither supports nor opposes anything. Hollingsworth 1980 and Barreteau 1988 use 'stress/accent' for different objects: Barreteau's accent d'intensité is an automatic, non-distinctive intensity accent (with vowel tensing) on the final syllable of the phonological word before pause; Hollingsworth's 'stress' is a speaker-assigned focal super-high pitch on one word per utterance, predictable in narrative from a grammatical-category ranking, with no fixed word-level position given (he explicitly says he lacks data to state rules at word level). Hollingsworth's observation that the utterance-final syllable is the lowest in pitch and usually falling concerns intonation, not intensity, and does not conflict with Barreteau's final intensity accent. The catalog's word-level statement (final-syllable, automatic, non-contrastive, per Barreteau 1988) stands unchanged.
